title: Maximus' good cheer
hook: from Maximus: self-command, cheerfulness in illness, doing duties without complaint (Meditations 1.15)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Severus, and the idea of a state with one law and equal speech. Your line was equal voices. Whose opinion did you let finish? Day five hundred twenty-nine.

Some people can't empty the dishwasher without a soundtrack of sighs. Others just do it. And now and then you meet someone who does the dull job, the hard job, even the job they're too sick for, and somehow makes the room lighter while they do it. What lingers afterward is less what they said than the air around them. Marcus had a friend like that, a senator and Stoic named Claudius Maximus, and he gave him a long, detailed portrait in book one. Today: Maximus' good cheer.
screen: `A SOUNDTRACK OF SIGHS.` → `THE ONE WHO MAKES THE ROOM LIGHTER.` → `MAXIMUS' GOOD CHEER.`

segments.voice: First, who he was. Claudius Maximus was a Roman senator and a Stoic. He governed the province of Africa, and history happens to remember him as the judge at a famous trial there, where the writer Apuleius was accused of using magic to win a rich wife. Apuleius's speech in his own defense still survives. Second, the portrait. From Maximus, Marcus says, he learned to govern himself and not be pushed off course by anything. To be cheerful in every circumstance, illnesses included. To mix gentleness and dignity in the right measure. And to do the work set in front of him without complaining. Third, the details. Everyone believed that Maximus meant what he said, and that whatever he did, he did without bad intent. He never seemed astonished or rattled, never rushed, never put things off, never lost heart, and never laughed to cover up irritation. He was quick to do good and quick to forgive. And Marcus adds a lovely line: nobody ever felt looked down on by Maximus, and nobody ever dared think himself better than him. Fourth, cheer without complaint. Notice that the cheerfulness and the not-complaining sit together. Complaint is often the sound of carrying something while making sure everyone knows how heavy it is. Maximus carried it, and kept the weight to himself, so the people around him could breathe easier. Later in the notebook, Marcus writes simply that Maximus died. Book one keeps him as Marcus saw him: doing the job in front of him, cheerfully, without a word about how hard it was.
screen: `CLAUDIUS MAXIMUS, SENATOR AND JUDGE.` · `CHEERFUL, EVEN WHEN ILL.` · `NO RUSH, NO DELAY, NO FAKE LAUGH.` · `CARRY IT, KEEP THE WEIGHT QUIET.` · then, large: `NO COMPLAINT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one duty waiting for you today that you'd usually grumble about. The laundry. The expense report. The call you've been dodging. Picture yourself doing it. Now picture doing it the way Maximus might have: not grinning falsely, just steady, unhurried, without the sighs. Notice what changes for the people near you. Breathe with that picture. The bell holds the time.
Claudius Maximus. The Roman senator and Stoic who did his duties without complaint, cheerful even in illness, so no one near him felt small. Today's word.
Your line: no complaint. Do one duty today from start to finish without a single complaint, out loud or in a message. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations take Maximus as a model for doing tedious or hard tasks steadily and without complaint, especially when tired or unwell.
